questions.title: Gravitational potential & field of Mars — satellite orbit

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer:
The work done per unit mass
in moving a small test mass from infinity to the point.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
The satellite moves from r₁ = (3.4 + 1.7) × 10⁶ = 5.1 × 10⁶ m to r₂ = (3.4 + 6.8) × 10⁶ = 10.2 × 10⁶ m from the centre of Mars. Using ΔEP = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂):
5.1 × 10⁸ = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × M × 122 × [(5.1 × 10⁶)⁻¹ − (10.2 × 10⁶)⁻¹]
M = 6.4 × 10²³ kg

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: The satellite stays over the same point of Mars, so its period equals Mars’s rotation period: Mars takes (just under) 25 hours to rotate once on its axis.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: The orbit is equatorial, and/or the satellite orbits in the same direction as the rotation of Mars.

questions.title: Helium atom model — Coulomb’s law, electron orbits & field strength

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The (electric) force between two point charges is (directly) proportional to the product of their charges and inversely proportional to the square of their separation.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The helium nucleus contains two protons, so its charge is +2e.

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer:
The electric force provides the centripetal force: F = mv²/r, so
v = √(Fr/m) = √(1.6 × 10⁻⁸ × 170 × 10⁻¹² / 9.11 × 10⁻³¹)
= 1.7 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer:
v = 2πr/T, so T = 2πr/v = 2π × 170 × 10⁻¹² / (1.7 × 10⁶)
= 6.2 × 10⁻¹⁶ s
(Equivalently F = 4π²mr/T² gives the same period.)

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.answer:
E ∝ Q/r². The other electron has charge e at a distance of 340 pm, and the nucleus has charge 2e at 170 pm, so
ratio = [e/(340 × 10⁻¹²)²]/[2e/(170 × 10⁻¹²)²] = (170)²/(2 × 340)² = 0.13

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.answer: The other electron exerts a small repulsive force, so the resultant inward force is slightly less than 1.6 × 10⁻⁸ N — hence the speed of the electron is slightly lower (or its period slightly greater).

questions.title: Specific latent heat — vaporisation vs fusion & ice–water mixture

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The (thermal) energy per unit mass required to change state at constant temperature.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: Vaporisation involves a much larger increase in the separation (or volume) of the molecules than fusion, so much more work has to be done against the intermolecular forces — a much larger increase in molecular potential energy. Since the kinetic energy of the molecules is unchanged in either change of state, more thermal energy is needed to vaporise a substance.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
Heat lost by the water = heat to melt the ice + heat to warm the melted water. Using Q = mcΔθ and Q = mL:
(37.0 × L) + (37.0 × 4.18 × 10.3) = 208 × 4.18 × (26.4 − 10.3)
37.0L + 1593 = 14000
L = 335 J g⁻¹

questions.title: Internal energy & the first law of thermodynamics

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The sum of the (randomly distributed) kinetic and potential energies of the particles of the system — the total energy of the random motion of its particles.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: For an ideal gas there are no intermolecular forces, so the potential energy is zero and the internal energy equals the total kinetic energy of the molecules. The average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to the (thermodynamic) temperature, so the internal energy is directly proportional to the thermodynamic temperature.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer:
Compression (T → 3T): internal energy rises threefold, so ΔU = +2U; work done on the gas = +W. From the first law ΔU = q + W, so thermal energy supplied q = 2U − W.
Cooling at constant volume (3T → 2T): work done = 0; the internal energy falls from 3U to 2U, so ΔU = −U; hence thermal energy supplied q = ΔU = −U.

questions.title: Floating block — simple harmonic motion & energy

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The oscillation extends from h = 0.8 m to h = 2.0 m about the equilibrium at h = 1.4 m, so the amplitude = 0.60 m.

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: The line is a straight line through the origin, showing a ∝ −(displacement), so the oscillations are simple harmonic.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: Any three of: the mean/equilibrium position is at h = 1.4 m; the total energy of the oscillations is 9.0 J; the angular frequency is 1.2 rad s⁻¹ (period 5.1 s, or frequency 0.19 Hz); the maximum speed is 0.73 m s⁻¹; the mass of the block is 33 kg.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer: A U-shaped curve resting on the h-axis (minimum at EP = 0), drawn between h = 0.8 m and h = 2.0 m with the minimum at h = 1.4 m and both end-points at EP = 9.0 J (since EP = total energy − EK).

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.answer: The conversion of an alternating current (a.c.) into a direct current (d.c.).

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.answer: To smooth the rectified output (reduce the ripple).

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer:
A = 12 V (the peak value), and B = 2π/T = 2π/(20 × 10⁻³)
= 310 rad s⁻¹

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: Full-wave rectification (both halves of each cycle are used).

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: Four diodes connected as a bridge rectifier — a diamond/lattice of four diodes (each with the correct circuit symbol), with the a.c. input connected across one diagonal and the output taken across the other.

parts.label: (b)(iv)
parts.answer:
During discharge V = V₀e^(−t/τ). From Fig. 6.2 the p.d. falls from 12 V to 8.0 V in 7.3 ms:
8.0 = 12e^(−7.3 × 10⁻³/τ)
τ = −7.3 × 10⁻³/ln(8.0/12) = 0.018 s

questions.title: Magnetic fields — flux density, force & velocity selector

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: Magnetic flux density is the force per unit length per unit current acting on a (straight) conductor placed perpendicular to the field.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: F = BQv (with the velocity perpendicular to the magnetic field).

parts.label: (b)(ii)
parts.answer: An arrow at Y pointing vertically upwards (from Fleming’s left-hand rule for a positive charge).

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: A circular path curving upwards through the field (the force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it acts as a centripetal force).

parts.label: (c)(i)
parts.answer: Apply an electric field vertically downwards so that the electric force on the particle is in the opposite direction to the magnetic force. The particle then passes straight through to Z when the magnitudes of the electric and magnetic forces are equal.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: EQ = BQv, so v = E/B.

questions.title: Electron & positron — de Broglie wavelength & annihilation

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The wavelength associated with a moving particle.

parts.label: (c)
parts.answer:
Similarity: they have the same mass (or the same magnitude of charge, or both are leptons).
Difference: the electron has negative charge while the positron has positive charge (the positron is the antiparticle of the electron).

parts.label: (d)(i)
parts.answer: Annihilation (a particle–antiparticle reaction).

parts.label: (d)(ii)
parts.answer: The electron and positron disappear — their mass is converted into energy, and this mass–energy becomes the energy of the two gamma-ray photons.

parts.label: (d)(iii)
parts.answer: Two photons are produced travelling in opposite directions so that momentum is conserved (the initial total momentum is zero).

parts.label: (d)(v)
parts.answer:
Each of the two gamma photons carries the rest energy of one particle plus its kinetic energy:
E = mc² + Ek = 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ × (3.00 × 10⁸)² + 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ = 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁴ J.
Using E = hc/λ:
λ = hc/E = (6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3.00 × 10⁸)/(8.3 × 10⁻¹⁴) = 2.39 × 10⁻¹² m

questions.title: Radioactive decay — activity, decay constant & half-life

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The number of nuclear disintegrations per unit time.

parts.label: (b)
parts.answer: The activity is proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei (A = λN), and the activity equals the rate of decrease of N, so dN/dt = −λN — the number of nuclei falls at a rate proportional to itself, giving an exponential variation.

parts.label: (c)(ii)
parts.answer: Half-life = ln 2/λ = ln 2/0.048 = 14 min

parts.label: (c)(iii)
parts.answer: An exponential decay curve starting at (0, 180 Bq), with a negative gradient that decreases in magnitude, passing through (8.4, 120) and (14, 90), and approaching the t-axis by t = 24 min.

parts.label: (a)
parts.answer: The speed of recession of a galaxy is (directly) proportional to its distance from the observer (v = H₀d), where the speed is that of the galaxy receding from the observer and d is its distance from the observer.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.answer: The observed wavelength is longer than the emitted wavelength (red-shifted), so the galaxy is receding from the Earth (the Doppler shift of the light).

parts.label: (b)(iii)
parts.answer: The wavelength of maximum intensity is inversely proportional to the temperature (Wien’s law). The observed wavelength is too high (red-shifted), so the determined temperature is too low compared with the true value.
